Churlish
CHURL-ish
adj. (rude and ungenerous; hard in dealing; the character of Nabal)
From Old English ceorl, a common freeman, which drifted into meaning a boor. The Authorized Version uses it once, of Nabal the Carmelite, who is introduced as churlish and evil in his doings in the same sentence that praises his wife.

Biblical Definition

Now the name of the man was Nabal; and the name of his wife Abigail: and she was a woman of good understanding, and of a beautiful countenance: but the man was churlish and evil in his doings. The contrast is the hinge of the chapter. David's men had protected Nabal's shepherds in the wilderness and asked at sheepshearing for whatever came to hand; Nabal's answer is a small masterpiece of self-regard, with the pronoun repeated: Shall I then take my bread, and my water, and my flesh that I have killed for my shearers, and give it unto men, whom I know not whence they be? Abigail intercepted four hundred armed men with loaves, wine, sheep, parched corn, raisins, and figs, and with a speech that named her husband honestly — as his name is, so is he; Nabal is his name, and folly is with him — and that recalled David from a slaughter he had sworn to commit. David's reply is the verdict on the whole episode: Blessed be the LORD God of Israel, which sent thee this day to meet me. Nabal's heart died within him ten days later, and the LORD smote him.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): rude; surly; austere; sullen; rough in temper; unfeeling; uncivil; also, selfish; narrow-minded; avaricious.

expand to see more

CHURLISH, a. Rude; surly; austere; sullen; rough in temper; unfeeling; uncivil.

CHURLISH, a. Selfish; narrow-minded; avaricious.

CHURL, n. A rustic; a countryman or laborer; a rough, surly, ill-bred man.

LIBERALITY, n. Largeness of mind; catholic principles; generosity; munificence.

FOLLY, n. Weakness of intellect; imbecility of mind; want of understanding; in Scripture, criminal weakness; depravity of mind.

Key Scripture

1Sa 25:3 — "Now the name of the man was Nabal; and the name of his wife Abigail: and she was a woman of good understanding, and of a beautiful countenance: but the man was churlish and evil in his doings; and he was of the house of Caleb."

1Sa 25:11 — "Shall I then take my bread, and my water, and my flesh that I have killed for my shearers, and give it unto men, whom I know not whence they be?"

1Sa 25:25 — "Let not my lord, I pray thee, regard this man of Belial, even Nabal: for as his name is, so is he; Nabal is his name, and folly is with him: but I thine handmaid saw not the young men of my lord, whom thou didst send."

1Sa 25:32 — "And David said to Abigail, Blessed be the LORD God of Israel, which sent thee this day to meet me:"

Modern Corruption

Ungenerous hardness is defended as prudence and as a right over one's own property; Scripture names Nabal's reasoning folly and puts his name on it, while commending the wife who acted over his head to prevent bloodshed.

expand to see more

Nabal's refusal was legally unimpeachable. The bread was his, the water was his, the flesh was killed for his shearers, and he owed David nothing by contract. Scripture calls him a man of Belial and folly all the same, because the biblical doctrine of property has never been absolute ownership. The land was the LORD's, the corners of the field belonged to the poor by statute, and the whole law assumes that a man's goods are held in trust with obligations attached. My bread, my water, my flesh, is the grammar of a fool, and the chapter says so.

Abigail's part requires care and the dictionary gives it plainly. She acted without telling her husband, contradicted his decision, and is commended by David and by the narrator. Submission in Scripture is never a mandate to assist in sin or to stand by while blood is shed; Abigail intervened to prevent a massacre and to keep David from avenging himself, and she did it with humility, courage, and remarkable theological skill, reminding him that the LORD would make him a sure house and that he should not have this as a grief of heart, that thou hast shed blood causeless. Her example is the standing answer to anyone who reads headship as a licence for folly.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew qasheh (H7186), hard, harsh, churlish; nabal (H5036), foolish, senseless, and so the man's name; nebalah (H5039), folly.

expand to see more

Hebrew qasheh (H7186) — hard, severe, harsh; the man was churlish.

Hebrew nabal (H5036) — foolish, senseless, base; Nabal is his name, and folly is with him.

Hebrew nebalah (H5039) — folly, disgraceful wickedness; the noun behind the name.

Hebrew sekel (H7922) — discretion, good sense; a woman of good understanding.

Hebrew ra' (H7451) — evil, bad; evil in his doings.

Usage

"“the man was churlish and evil in his doings” — the single occurrence."

"“Shall I then take my bread, and my water” — the grammar of the fool."

"“Blessed be the LORD God of Israel, which sent thee this day” — David on Abigail."
